newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada has more than one bid for DBS satellites.
newsitem.headline: Canada has more than one bid for DBS satellites.

text.p: The government of Canada has received more than one application for permission to develop and operate direct broadcast satellites, a government spokesman said on Monday. They would be used to get Canada's direct-to-home television services off the ground.
Telesat Canada, 57 percent owned by BCE Inc, announced it had submitted a proposal on Monday in response to a call on November 7 from Industry Minister John Manley.
Manley spokesman Bill Milliken said more than one application was in and officials had been informed others were on their way. The deadline was close of business on Monday.
Milliken was unable to name companies on Monday.
Manley's office had said companies would have until February 28 to submit their proposals.

But if a company already had a DBS satellite or sufficient DBS capacity to meet interim Canadian needs, it would be considered for fast-track licensing. Applications for the fast track were due on December 16.

Manley's decision to invite Canadian bids for the use of a Canadian orbital slot came after the U.S. Federal Communications Commission denied a bid by two U.S. companies to beam programs across North America through two satellites which were to be owned and operated by Telesat Canada.
Those two U.S. companies were TelQuest Ventures and Tele-Communications Inc.
In addition to BCE's 57 percent share, Telesat is also owned by Canadian phone companies and Spar Aerospace Ltd.
Expressvu Inc, partly owned by BCE, has regulatory approval to operate DTH television but has been stymied partly by lack of satellite capacity.
Power DirecTv, 80 percent owned by Power Corp of Canada, also won a license but decided against launching it at least for now.
A unit of Direct Choice T.V. Inc won a third license, and Tee-Comm Electronics Inc also filed for approval to launch a DTH service.
